questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I chose Munich as my exchange destination initially because of personal connections to the city both through friends and language, but it also checked a lot of other important boxes for me such as 
-great university
-safe, green city, good public transport
-welcoming people and culture

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was quite easy, the staff at LMU were very helpful and easy to contact via email. It might have been a little more complicated to get information if I weren't fluent in german.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Assistance via email by the exchange department, and by certain professors if I had questions regarding their courses. I also participated in a LMU Buddy program, where I was assigned an older student to help me with questions which worked very well. Else I got assistance from fellow students in my classes if needed.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It is quite hard to find accommodations, as the university only has very limited available student housing, and it is not on campus. I personally found accommodation through friends. So I would definitely ask around if anyone has connections to Munich, and else it could work to make a good profile on
wg-gesucht.de

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Everybody lives off campus in Munich. It will be practical for you to try to find somewhere that is close to the metro lines U3/06 if you live a little further from the city center, as they go directly to the main campus of LMU ("Universität"). It isn't cheap to rent in Munich although it is not too bad compared to Copenhagen.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I haven't met anyone receiving housing through the university, although I mainly interacted with non-Erasmus students. I think they can only cover 25% of exchange students or something in that ballpark.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Not difficult but different to Copenhagen. The difficult part was getting the courses approved from home beforehand

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: At LMU, you don't register for courses other than adding them to your curriculum online (LSF). You can change courses at any time during the semester, and the only binding registration is for exams towards the end of the semester. You also register for most of the exams online.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: It was explained during lectures/on slides, and in emails from the university.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Successful. Be aware that some courses are only available during either the winter or summer term.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Try to get pre-approved a lot of different subjects before you go to Munich, as their semesters start very late and the course catalogues mostly aren't available in time for when you first apply for pre-approval. Also, then you will have flexibility and be able to easier switch courses if there are some that you don't like.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level is pretty high for third year Bachelor courses. They expect you to be able to apply a lot of knowledge by heart from math/statistics/econometrics/micro and macro I and II in most electives. The exams are very time-pressured and all of my exams were written by hand and closed book.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Most courses on BA-level consist of lecture + tutorial, similar to UCPH. People participate more in the lectures, which is really nice in my opinion. The tutorials are mostly taught by PHD students, and they are bigger than at UCPH. Mostly, you will go through exercises together, and the TA guides you all the way through.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Game Theory (Micro III)
Environmental and Resource Economics
Economics of Education
Geography and Technology in Economic History
Modulprüfung Grundlagen der Wirtschaftspsychologie

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The two courses in Economic History taught by Professor Cantoni are absolutely amazing. In the summer term, the class focuses on culture and institutions, and in the winter term it is on geography and technology. I have had them both pre-approved as Economic History at UCPH. Game Theory is also good and works as Micro III but the exam is really difficult.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: None come to mind

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Public transport is very cheap if you get the 29 euro ticket for students. Eating out is also fairly cheap even though it is more expensive than other parts in Germany. Most books are accessible through an online library from the University, so I didn't buy any books.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are a few bigger parties organized by students at the university, and also sports clubs etc. but I didn't use those so unfortunately can't provide as much additional information than what the exchange staff send you.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend going to concerts at the Isarphilharmonie, Herkulessaal or the Opera. Swimming in the Isar in summer is also lovely, and visiting the Christkindlmarkt in December. Of course the Oktoberfest also takes place just before the winter semester starts! Going to the English garden, or museums like Haus der Kunst and Lenbachhaus. If you like surfing, check out the Eisbachwelle, where you can surf in the middle of the city.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Going on a hike or to ski in the mountains nearby, or go to one of the bigger lakes in the area (Starnberger See, Ammersee,...). A day trip to Salzburg is also lovely, or if you have more time, even go to Vienna or Prague! MESA (the Erasmus network in Munich) organises a lot of these trips.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: For me it was very easy as I am born and raised in Switzerland, so language wasn't an issue and the culture is fairly similar. I have only experienced welcoming and lovely people, although I am told that (especially the older generation) can be quite direct and maybe a little "impolite" at times, but I didn't get this impression. You might be surprised as a Scandinavian how common cash still is, and how a lot of things aren't quite as digitalized as in Denmark.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I have had great experiences just starting a conversation with people from my courses etc. , they are super kind and helpful. Also bumble bff is a great way to meet friends, local and non-local.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I had to get used to bring cash with me, and that supermarkets are closed on sundays and quite a few holidays that we don't have in Denmark. Also, most close at 8pm. German people are quite busy and often work late, so finding time to see your friends might be easier if you plan a little ahead.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: People are very genuine, caring and helpful, and you don't feel like you have to be a certain way to fit in with them. I love the WG-culture (living in shared apartments as students), that is even more prevalent than in Copenhagen. If possible, I really recommend you to find a room in a WG, it's a great way to find friends.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
-Solutions to tutorial-exercises are not uploaded, so try to ask other students if you can't be present
-Use the roomfinder in the online portal LSF to find your lecture/tutorial. The buildings are very big!
-I would recommend to take notes with a tablet and an "Apple pencil" or similar, as they do a lot of things by hand and it will be the fastest way to do it, especially in tutorials where they write a lot of formulas by hand. And it will prepare you better for the exam form, where you will have to write everything on paper.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: You have to use your student card to buy food in the canteen (first, you have to put money on it on site, most places require cash). You can reserve library spots at your faculty online, and this is crucial to do if you want to secure a spot to study during exams. A lot of exams are written almost immediately after the last lecture is held, and I had 5 exams in 9 days, so try and stay up to date with the courses during the semester or catch up in the christmas holiday, which is quite long. It's also important to note that the semesters start very late and end late, so in my case I missed the first week of my new semester in Copenhagen when I got home.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Feeling home in a new place, meeting new people and forming lasting friendships. Exploring a new city and getting to know it. Attending interesting lectures.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The exams are clearly very different and challenging

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I had a great experience in Munich and would recommend it to anyone who doesn't mind studying a bit while on exchange;)

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
